messages.author: 00a93903438789e4
messages.subject: Diverse problems using sem() function
parts:
Hello everyone,

I am currently encountering numerous problems while trying to fit nested models using sem() function.

For instance, the addition of one single observed variable can prevent the convergence of a model, give negative variances, or make the covariance matrix of latent variables not positive definite...

Even worse, I recently noticed that a change in the order of manifest variables in a latent variable description prevents the model of converging, while it converges after 180 iterations when the exact same observed variables are in an other order...

Is such an instability frequent, and what can explain it? Am I doing something wrong?

Here is the code that describes my most complex model, which converges but gives negative variances (some of -30 or even -40) and uncomputable standard errors.

>model_compl = '
    Topo =~ Strahler + BV + Alt
    Qual =~ Ammo + Azo + Carbo + Condu + DBO5 + MES + Nitra + Nitri + Ortho + Oxy + Phos + pH + Satu + Temp
    Frag =~ Barr_10km + Seu_10km + Home_range
    Flux =~ Deb_min + Pen + Dist_emb + Deb
    Land_use =~ Arti + Ara_perm + Prai + Hetero + Nat

    Arti ~~ Ara_perm
    Prai ~~ Nat
    Ammo ~~ Nitri
    Nitra ~~ Phos + Ortho
    Carbo ~~ DBO5
    Phos ~~ Ortho
    Home_range ~~ Barr_10km + Seu_10km
   
    Ar ~ Topo + Qual + Frag + Flux + Land_use
'
>fit_compl = sem(model_compl, data = data_norm, verbose = T, fixed.x = F)
>summary(fit_compl, standardized = T, fit.measures = T, rsquare = F)

Thanks in advance for your help !

Lisa

parts:
On 04/25/2013 02:48 PM, lisa.f...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hello everyone,
>
> I am currently encountering numerous problems while trying to fit nested
> models using sem() function.
>
> For instance, the addition of one single observed variable can prevent
> the convergence of a model, give negative variances, or make the
> covariance matrix of latent variables not positive definite...
This smells like model misspecification.

> Even worse, I recently noticed that a change in the order of manifest
> variables in a latent variable description prevents the model of
> converging, while it converges after 180 iterations when the exact same
> observed variables are in an other order...

If you change the order of the indicators, you choose a different
reference indicator (by default the first indicator). Usually, this does
not matter, unless the chosen reference indicator is a (very) poor
indicator of the latent variable.

> Is such an instability frequent, and what can explain it? Am I doing
> something wrong?

My impression is that your measurement model is shaky. If you remove the
regression, do you have a good model fit? Do all indicators have
significant factor loadings? Do the standardized factor loadings differ
in magnitude?

If you want me to investigate this further (or run it through a
commercial program), I would need your data and a full R script.

Yves.

messages.author: 00a93903438789e4
messages.subject: Re: Diverse problems using sem() function
parts:
Thank you very much for your reply!

Ok, I now understand better the importance of the order of indicators. The thing is that the first indicator mentioned in the latent variables definitions was often a poor one, so I guess it explains some of my difficulties.
So I removed all the non-significant indicators, as well as one of the latent variables, which was obviously creating a lot of convergence and not positive definite matrix problems (even if I still don't really understand why...).

With all these modifications, I managed to obtain a model where all the P(>|z|) are smaller than 0.05, the standardized factor loadings range from -0.6 to 1.4, but some estimated variances are still negative (even if it is with small values like -0.17, which are quite far from the -40 of my precedent model!). Any idea of what could explain that, or what I could do to prevent it?

Thanks!

Lisa

> With all these modifications, I managed to obtain a model where all the
> P(>|z|) are smaller than 0.05, the standardized factor loadings range
> from -0.6 to 1.4, but some estimated variances are still negative (even
> if it is with small values like -0.17, which are quite far from the -40
> of my precedent model!). Any idea of what could explain that, or what I
> could do to prevent it?

Hard to say. It could be the data, the model, or both. The best solution
is to revise the model so that there are no negative variances. If that
is difficult, another approach is to 'label' the variance (using, say,
the label 'v1'), and add an inequality constraint:

v1 > 0

Yves.

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Diverse problems using sem() function
parts:
On 05/12/2013 02:23 AM, John Marx wrote:
> Hello Yves,
>
> sorry to bother you with a simple question:

> How looks the syntax for your solution?

Well, as a minimal example:

model <- ' f =~ x1 + x2 + x3
# label residual variances
x1 ~~ v1*x1
x2 ~~ v2*x2
x3 ~~ v3*x3
# constraints
v1 > 0
v2 > 0
v3 > 0
'

Yves.
